article_title: Human-AI Collaboration for Qualitative Analysis in Participatory Design: Refining the Writing Analytics Tool
citation: Potter, A.; Serhan, Z.; Patne, N. A.; Öncel, P.; Ahmed, I.; Arner, T.; Islam, R.; Roscoe, R. D.; Allen, L. A.; Crossley, S. A.; McNamara, D. S. (2026). title: Why–When–How feedback framework for presenting writing metrics
description: WAT-C presents each advanced metric's written feedback in a Why–When–How structure: "The Why section explains the rationale for the feedback", the When section "describes situations or genres where the writing behavior is most appropriate", and the How section "provides concrete revision strategies students can apply to improve their work". The pattern operationalizes feedback principles holding that effective feedback details both the task and improvement strategies, aiming to make advanced analytics interpretable, actionable, and instructionally relevant for student revision.
requirements: Underlying metrics with defined levels and revision guidance so each Why, When, and How component can be populated
constraints: Instructors in the focus groups critiqued the clarity, tone, and contextual relevance of the feedback comments, prompting revisions
target_learners: College writing students reviewing automated feedback on essays
target_learning_goals: Interpreting metric feedback, understanding communicative context, and performing meaningful revisions
examples: For Word Variety, students read why lexical diversity enhances engagement, when to prioritize consistency over variation, and how to revise by replacing repeated words with synonyms.

article_title: Understanding and Supporting District Systems Change Around Computer Science Education
citation: Quinn Burke, Jeremy Roschelle, Pati Ruiz, & Josh Weisgrau. (2021). Understanding and Supporting District Systems Change Around Computer Science Education. AERA Annual Conference, Division L Structured Poster Session. https://bit.ly/36szXLy
title: Three-step district pathway design sequence: Why, What, How
description: The toolkit structures district CS/CT pathway design as a three-step sequence. Step 1 articulates the Why through vision, foundations, and strategic alignment; Step 2 defines and communicates the What by identifying core CT competencies for each grade band; Step 3 establishes the How by naming district leaders, planning professional learning, and setting measurements such as using look fors, surveys to benchmark progress in classrooms. Pilot districts' progress is tracked against these steps in a progress table.
requirements: District leadership engagement and a planning team
constraints: Progress table shows districts at different stages, with several steps still in progress
target_learners: K-12 students district-wide
target_learning_goals: System-wide CT and CS learning pathways
examples: Broward County FL and North Salem NY show completed vision, alignment, and competency steps with measurement underway, while Vandalia IL and Kettle Moraine WI are earlier in the sequence

article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts
citation: Guckenburg, S., Hurley, N., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts. San Francisco: WestEd. http://jprc.wested.org/
title: Implement restorative justice as a whole-school integrated approach rather than a stand-alone program
description: The majority of experts agreed RJ should be integrated within a broader school culture in which everyone uses the same language and techniques. Stand-alone disciplinary approaches with minimal training "may have less positive impact than a whole-school approach." Some suggested teachers begin using RJ in staff meetings and with each other before introducing it to students.
requirements: The entire school environment must be restorative in its approach to students, staff, parents, and community members for RJ to be sustainable or successful
constraints: Simplified models that appear easier to implement may win administrator buy-in but were cautioned against by experts
target_learners: All students, staff, and administrators in a school community
target_learning_goals: School culture change
consistent restorative language and techniques
examples: Experts suggested teachers practice RJ in staff meetings and with each other before introducing it to students
key_sources: Guckenburg, S., Hurley, N., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: Summary Findings from Interviews with Experts. San Francisco: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED568378

article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review
citation: Fronius, Darling-Hammond, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2019). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review. WestEd Justice & Prevention Research Center. http://jprc.wested.org/
title: Integrate restorative justice school- and district-wide rather than as an add-on program to sustain it
description: This principle holds that RJ practices work best when embedded in a school's overall philosophy and formal policy rather than run as a bolt-on program. The review states that "one way to sustain RJ practices is to integrate them across the school and district rather than having RJ be an add-on program," and that such integration is often described as "Whole School Restorative Justice." Oakland research is cited as suggesting integration is more effective across a range of outcomes than reaction-based practices alone.
requirements: District integration of the RJ approach into formal policy and procedures, with decisions about discipline considering multiple stakeholders including teachers, administrators, youth, parents, and community members
constraints: The review notes this implementation information is not backed by rigorous scientific evidence such as randomized controlled trials supporting causal claims about which steps are helpful or essential
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Improved school climate, reduced exclusionary discipline, and sustained restorative practice implementation
examples: The review cites Oakland research (Jain et al., 2014) suggesting integration throughout the school is substantially more effective than limited, reaction-based RJ practices, and a Detroit district leveraging Title I funding to hire a full-time RJ coordinator.
key_sources: Fronius, Darling-Hammond, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2019). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review. WestEd Justice & Prevention Research Center. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED595733

article_title: Serving the Whole Person: An Alignment and Coherence Guide for Local Education Agencies
citation: Walrond, N. (2021). Serving the whole person: An alignment and coherence guide for local education agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/whole-person-alignment-and-coherence-guide-for-local-education-agencies
title: Whole-person development as integrated physiological, cognitive, social, and emotional domains
description: The guide defines serving the whole person as a comprehensive view of human development spanning multiple interrelated domains. It states that "Science shows that these domains develop together, and that health and well-being in one domain bolster the health and well-being of the others," citing Cantor et al. (2018), and that integrated approaches yield improved outcomes, citing Durlak et al. (2011) and Carneiro et al. (2007). Serving the whole person is presented as the foundation for outcomes such as success in school and the workplace, engaged citizenship, healthy relationships, personal purpose, and a sense of place in the community.
requirements: Whole-person efforts must be tailored to students' strengths, aspirations, and needs for students to develop to their full potential, as the guide states
constraints: The guide attributes the domain-integration evidence to cited external research rather than testing it itself
target_learners: K-12 students
the adults who care for them
target_learning_goals: cognitive, physiological, social, and emotional development leading to equitable outcomes
examples: The guide lists five general outcomes of serving the whole person: success in school and the workplace, engaged citizenship, healthy relationships, personal purpose, and a sense of place in the community

article_title: Teaching for Powerful Learning: Lessons from Gateway Public Schools
citation: Cook-Harvey, C. M., Flook, L., Efland, E., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2020). Teaching for powerful learning: Lessons from Gateway Public Schools. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/social-and-emotional-learning-case-study-gateway
title: Framework for Whole Child Education: four principles from the science of learning and development
description: The report organizes its findings around a synthesis of science-of-learning-and-development research identifying four major principles: supportive environments, productive instructional strategies, social and emotional development, and systems of support. It states that "Supportive environments promote secure attachments and relationships, a sense of safety and belonging, and relational trust" and that the four principles "characterize the practices observed at Gateway Middle School and Gateway High School." The framework is depicted in Figure 1 and mapped to specific Gateway practices in Table 3.
requirements: Practices must work in tandem across all four areas, since the report notes each structure works with the others for mission-driven coherence
constraints: The framework is a synthesis framing drawn from a prior research review, applied interpretively to one case study school
target_learners: K-12 students in diverse public schools
students with learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: whole child academic, social-emotional, and identity development
self-regulation and perseverance
learning how to learn
examples: Table 3 maps Gateway practices such as advisories, inquiry-based instruction, restorative supports, and multi-tiered systems of support onto the four principles

article_title: Supporting Students Experiencing Homelessness: District Approaches to Supports and Funding
citation: Levin, S., Espinoza, D., & Griffith, M. (2022). Supporting students experiencing homelessness: District approaches to supports and funding. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/557.894
title: Whole child approach to supporting students experiencing homelessness, grounded in the science of learning and development
description: The report frames students experiencing homelessness as having interrelated physical, emotional, and academic needs that signal "a need for a whole child approach to supporting them." It holds that "Such an approach is consistent with the science of learning and development, which shows that stability, consistency, trust, and belonging are foundational to effective learning." Under this account, homelessness harms learning through stress, instability, trauma, and school mobility that raise risks to health, social-emotional well-being, engagement, and achievement, so district supports must address nonacademic needs (housing, health, transportation, family stability) alongside academic services.
requirements: Coordination across district homeless programs, schools, and community-based organizations, with referral pathways into existing school-based supports for vulnerable students
constraints: The report states housing instability can negatively affect students even after the period of homelessness ends, and that addressing systemic causes of homelessness lies beyond districts' scope
target_learners: k–12 students experiencing homelessness, including unaccompanied youth
target_learning_goals: educational engagement, achievement, and attainment supported through stability, trust, and belonging
examples: Study districts folded students experiencing homelessness into existing school-based programs for vulnerable students, allowing homeless program staff to make referrals rather than provide all services directly
key_sources: Levin, S., Espinoza, D., & Griffith, M. (2022). Supporting students experiencing homelessness: District approaches to supports and funding. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/557.894

article_title: The Policy Deficit in AI × Social-Emotional Learning Research
citation: Tran Van Cuong, Liu Yihan, Nguyen Van Tuong. (2026). The Policy Deficit in AI x Social-Emotional Learning Research.
title: WH-question framework for decomposing policy implications into Who, What, Why, When/Where, and How
description: The review adapts a framework from Dello Russo et al. (2023) in which each policy implication is treated as "a short narrative that can be broken down into several parts": who it addresses, what actions it suggests, why they matter, when and where they apply, and how strongly they are framed (modal verbs such as must, should, could). The authors coded 31 implication narratives against these five dimensions, mapped onto their five research questions, using an a priori codebook refined through pilot coding with disagreement resolved in discussion with a third author.
requirements: Each distinct implication statement is treated as a single unit of analysis, allowing multiple codes within a dimension
constraints: Coding implicit policy implications can be subjective, as the authors state
target_learners: education researchers writing AI × SEL studies
target_learning_goals: writing evidence-grounded, actor-oriented policy implications
examples: The review coded 31 implication narratives from 18 papers, finding prescriptive framing in 24 claims and tentative framing in 7
key_sources: Tran Van Cuong, Liu Yihan, Nguyen Van Tuong. (2026). The Policy Deficit in AI x Social-Emotional Learning Research. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29950

article_title: Peer Instruction: Engaging Students One-on-One, All At Once
citation: Crouch, C. H., Watkins, J., Fagen, A. P., & Mazur, E. (2003). Peer Instruction: Engaging Students One-on-One, All At Once. Research-Based Reform of University Physics. https://scholar.google.com
title: Align every course element with active engagement, since gains are greatest when the questioning strategy is accompanied by other engagement strategies
description: The article reports that gains in student understanding are greatest when the PI questioning strategy is accompanied by other strategies that increase engagement, "so that every element of the course serves to involve students actively." This includes exams with both conceptual and quantitative questions, cooperative discussion sections, pre-class reading assignments, grading that rewards participation rather than correctness on ConcepTests, and an absolute grading scale to remove competition.
requirements: examinations should include both conceptual short essay and quantitative problem-solving questions because exams drive how students study
a cooperative classroom atmosphere, with students not graded on the correctness of ConcepTest answers
constraints: assigning pre-class reading, although helpful, is not required for using Peer Instruction
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory physics courses, including non-majors and physics majors
target_learning_goals: conceptual reasoning alongside quantitative problem solving, and sustained student engagement across all course components
examples: At Harvard the authors introduced free-response reading assignments and cooperative learning into discussion sections in 1996, and the normalized gain continued to rise as more course components were modified to engage students actively
key_sources: Crouch, C. H., Watkins, J., Fagen, A. P., & Mazur, E. (2003). Peer Instruction: Engaging Students One-on-One, All At Once. Research-Based Reform of University Physics. https://scholar.google.com

article_title: Examining the Effectiveness of School-Bullying Intervention Programs Globally: a Meta-analysis
citation: Hannah Gaffney, David P. Farrington, & Maria M. Ttofi. (2019). Examining the Effectiveness of School-Bullying Intervention Programs Globally: a Meta-analysis. International Journal of Bullying Prevention. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42380-019-0007-4
title: The whole-school approach to bullying prevention
description: The whole-school approach, first introduced by Dan Olweus in Norway, is an organizing framework for anti-bullying programs that "incorporates individuals involved in every aspect of students' lives," including peers, parents, teachers, and the wider community, not only the students involved in bullying. Programs such as KiVa and ViSC apply it with a socio-ecological theoretical framework. The meta-analysis found it "was not always the most effective": OBPP was highly effective, KiVa only marginally so, ViSC undesirable, while the non-whole-school NoTrap! was most effective for victimization.
requirements: Requires engagement of the whole school community: students, peers, parents, teachers, and the wider community
constraints: The article concludes the whole-school approach "might not be effective for every individual student," citing high-trajectory victimization participants who showed lesser decreases
target_learners: School children and adolescents aged 4 to 18
target_learning_goals: Reducing bullying perpetration and victimization in schools
examples: OBPP, KiVa, and ViSC all adopted the whole-school approach; NoTrap! instead used a peer-led online forum with trained student moderators.
key_sources: Hannah Gaffney, David P. Farrington, & Maria M. Ttofi. (2019). Examining the Effectiveness of School-Bullying Intervention Programs Globally: a Meta-analysis. International Journal of Bullying Prevention. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42380-019-0007-4

article_title: Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education
citation: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485
title: Plan graduate attribute assessment at whole-of-programme level with tasks extending beyond individual course boundaries
description: Because graduate attribute development occurs incrementally as students integrate learnings across a programme, the paper argues assessment must be planned programme-wide rather than course by course. It states that 'the development of graduate attributes requires a whole-of-programme approach to the planning of curriculum, teaching and assessment'. Where modular curricula dominate, assessors need openness to alternative and authentic forms such as capstone tasks that extend across traditional course boundaries.
requirements: Curriculum approach must permit programme-level planning; modular structures alone cannot capture attribute progression
constraints: Much graduate attribute progress is unlikely to be assessable within the time spans of courses or shorter modules
target_learners: university students in degree programmes
target_learning_goals: graduate attribute development and progression across a programme of study
examples: The paper points to 'high impact' and 'integrative' tasks used with paper-based or electronic portfolios as alternatives suited to programme-level attribute assessment
key_sources: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485

article_title: A critical period for second language acquisition: Evidence from 2/3 million English speakers
citation: Hartshorne Joshua K., Tenenbaum Joshua B., Pinker Steven. (2018). A critical period for second language acquisition: Evidence from 2/3 million English speakers. Cognition. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6559801/
title: WhichEnglish internet grammar quiz dataset (669,498 speakers)
description: An internet quiz at www.gameswithwords.org/WhichEnglish that presented 132 items (95 critical) covering phenomena such as "passivization, clefting, agreement, relative clauses, preposition use", plus dialect-distinguishing items used for recruiting. After exclusions, 669,498 participants aged 7-89 were analyzed across 38 languages with at least 1000 native speakers. Reliability for critical items was Chronbach's alpha = 0.86, and the dataset is available at http://osf.io/pyb8s.
requirements: Demographic questionnaire completion (about 80% of syntax completers)
Exclusion of inconsistent or implausible demographic responses
constraints: Analyses restricted to the 95 critical items
Written comprehension modality; production and oral modalities not tested

target_learning_goals: measuring syntactic knowledge across age of first exposure, current age, and years of experience
examples: Shared more than 300,000 times on Facebook; most common non-English native languages included Finnish (N = 39,962) and Turkish (N = 36,239)

article_title: Sharing Solutions: Persistence and Grounding in Multimodal Collaborative Problem Solving
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg, David Traum. (2006). Sharing solutions: persistence and grounding in multi-modal collaborative problem solving. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 15 (1), pp.121-151. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327809jls1501_9

description: The studied environment combines two media for computer-mediated collaborative problem solving: "a shared whiteboard and a MOO environment that includes a text chat facility." The whiteboard serves as a persistent shared workspace representing the state of problem solving, while the chat facility carries grounding exchanges about information created on the whiteboard. The setup enabled the exploratory study of acknowledgment rates and media use.

constraints: Studied in an exploratory setting with these two specific media; findings are interpreted for this configuration
target_learners: Pairs or groups collaborating in computer-mediated problem-solving tasks
target_learning_goals: Coordinating shared problem representations and grounding mutual understanding
examples: The whiteboard was used to represent the state of problem solving while chat grounded whiteboard content

article_title: Working Memory Capacity and the Development of Quantitative Central Conceptual Structures
citation: Morra, S.; Bisagno, E.; Caviola, S.; Delfante, C.; Mammarella, I. C. (2019). Working Memory Capacity and the Development of Quantitative Central Conceptual Structures. Cognition and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2019.1636797
title: Validated measure of the whole-number central conceptual structure
description: A validated instrument measuring children's whole-number central conceptual structure, developed and validated in Study I with 779 children from preschool to grade 5. The article reports that Study I "validated a measure of the whole number CCS", establishing that performance on it tracks working memory capacity in developmental-level units. It serves as the operational measure linking quantitative concept development to working memory in the article's tests of Case's theory.
requirements: Administered together with a working memory capacity measure to score developmental levels
target_learners: children from preschool to grade 5
target_learning_goals: whole number understanding

article_title: Reflecting on what counts as collaboration: Reaching forward without losing what is behind
citation: Sanna Järvelä, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2023). Reflecting on what counts as collaboration: Reaching forward without losing what is behind. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 18, 457–464. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09415-y
title: Collaboration as active, intentional, shared, effective communication toward a joint goal — the boundary question "what counts as collaboration"
description: The editorial centers on the question "What is the essence of collaboration?" and defines collaboration, following Dillenbourg (1999), as involving "individuals or groups working together to achieve common goals, share ideas, and contribute their efforts toward a collective objective or joint goal." The authors stress it is "active, intentional, shared, and effective communication and participation," and can be scripted and technology-supported. They use boundary cases — talking without a set learning objective, human–agent interaction, intersubjectivity with agents without minds — to push the field to elaborate its concepts as new themes (LA, AR/VR, GenAI) emerge.
requirements: The article presents this as a field-level boundary question that must be kept under active discussion when judging journal scope and integrating new paradigms.
target_learners: CSCL research community and learners in technology-supported collaborative environments
target_learning_goals: Understanding what qualifies an interaction as collaborative learning, including human–agent collaboration

article_title: Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science
citation: Rikke Magnussen, Yotam Hod. (2023). Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09641-9
title: What Is a Place? introductory module teaching the urban-developer perspective on city spaces
description: The What Is a Place? module was an introductory module developed by an urban development researcher at Aalborg University and a Danish learning platform developer to bridge skills between students and the professional urban development community. "The module comprised an introduction by the teacher or urban planning researcher and a five-minute video of Tivoli," a familiar Copenhagen amusement park. Students analyzed urban spaces using three questions about what can be measured and sensed, felt and valued, and explained, with an urban development researcher participating as a co-teacher leading the discussion.
requirements: An urban development researcher participating as a co-teacher throughout the module and leading the discussion
A familiar local place, such as the Tivoli video, that students can analyze with the three professional perspectives
constraints: Designed to introduce the skilled perspective of urban developers on city space, not to substitute for the full design-thinking process
target_learners: Students aged 11–15 in grades 5–9 in Copenhagen vulnerable-area schools
target_learning_goals: Applying the perspectives of urban developers in analyzing urban spaces, including senses, feelings, and the purpose or identity of a place
examples: In a fifth-grade class, students analyzing the Tivoli video described smells of popcorn, sounds of crowds, and mixed feelings of being annoyed and happy among many people
key_sources: Rikke Magnussen, Yotam Hod. (2023). Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09641-9

article_title: Exploring the effects of a musical play intervention on young children’s self-regulation and metacognition
citation: Zachariou, A., Bonneville-Roussy, A., Hargreaves, D., & Neokleous, R. (2023). Exploring the effects of a musical play intervention on young children's self-regulation and metacognition. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09342-1
title: Whitebread et al.'s three-area model of self-regulation and metacognition
description: The study adopts Whitebread et al.'s (2009) model, which "proposes three areas of self-regulation: metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive regulation and emotional and motivational regulation". Metacognitive knowledge covers knowledge of persons, tasks and strategies; metacognitive regulation covers planning, monitoring, control and evaluation; emotional/motivational regulation covers monitoring and control of emotional and motivational experiences. The model draws on the cognitive information-processing tradition (metamemory, metacognition) and the socio-cultural tradition (self-regulation), and underpins the C.Ind.Le coding framework and CHILD checklist used to measure all outcomes in this study.
requirements: Assessment requires coding verbal and non-verbal behaviours at utterance level, since metacognitive knowledge on-task relies only on children's verbalisations
constraints: On-task identification of metacognitive knowledge relies only on children's verbalisations, which the authors note may underestimate young children's abilities
target_learners: Young children in early primary school (aged 6)
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation and metacognition across cognitive, emotional, social and motivational domains
examples: The study coded Train Track Task observations and interview responses into the model's nine facets using the C.Ind.Le scheme, with inter-rater reliability ICC = .93

article_title: Racializing Motivation: A Race-Reimaged Framework of Belonging, Emoting, and Achieving Within STEM Higher Education Contexts
citation: Jessica T. DeCuir-Gunby, Paul A. Schutz, Saba L. Modaressi. (2026). Racializing Motivation: A Race-Reimaged Framework of Belonging, Emoting, and Achieving Within STEM Higher Education Contexts. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10220-w
title: White STEM spaces as racially hierarchical educational contexts that question minoritized students' belonging and competence
description: White STEM spaces emerge when racially minoritized students pursue STEM goals in white educational spaces whose "history, symbols, and traditions... replicate whiteness and white supremacy ideologies." For most white students these spaces seem normal, but for racially minoritized students, "white STEM spaces promote and make salient the presumed deficit ideological questions about whether racially minoritized students belong, are competent, and can be autonomous in those spaces." The construct is a core contextual element of the article's systems framework.
requirements: Analysis of minoritized students' experiences must account for the white-space character of STEM academic and work settings
constraints: The construct is developed for U.S. higher education STEM contexts
target_learners: Racially minoritized STEM students in predominantly white institutions
target_learning_goals: Understanding racialized barriers to belonging, competence beliefs, and autonomy in STEM spaces
examples: The article cites Anderson's observation that Black people are required to navigate white space as a condition of their existence

article_title: Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement
citation: Karel Kreijns, Kate Xu, Joshua Weidlich. (2022). Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09623-8
title: Whiteside and Garrett Dickers' Social Presence Model with five components for structuring online and blended courses
description: The review describes the social presence model (SPM) of Whiteside and Garrett Dickers, which sees social presence as 'a critical literacy for cultivating emotions and relationships' that serves an influential role in advancing and sustaining successful, meaningful learning experiences. The model is used to organize the structure of an online or blended course and encompasses five components: affective association, community cohesion, instructor involvement, interaction intensity, and knowledge and experience. The review positions it as a conceptualization that fits neither end of Lowenthal's continuum of social presence definitions.
requirements: The model is used to organize the structure of an online or blended course
constraints: The review notes this model cannot be placed on Lowenthal's social presence continuum because it treats social presence neither as a perception nor as an interpersonal connection
target_learners: students in online or blended courses
target_learning_goals: cultivating emotions and relationships to support meaningful learning experiences
examples: The five components include instructor involvement, defined as encouraging students to participate in higher order thinking and critical inquiry and developing relationships and social connections among students

article_title: Agency in Educational Technology: Interdisciplinary Perspectives and Implications for Learning Design
citation: Garvin Brod, Natalia Kucirkova, Joshua Shepherd, Dietsje Jolles, Inge Molenaar. (2023). Agency in Educational Technology: Interdisciplinary Perspectives and Implications for Learning Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09749-x
title: Wh-question design levers for agency in EdTech: what, who, when, and where choices can be made

article_title: Both individual and peer growth mindsets matter for academic resilience

title: What-matters-most framework of stigma domains: survival, social, and professional threats
description: The RESHAPE intervention is designed around a what-matters-most framework for understanding the origins of stigma among primary care practitioners, drawn from social neuroscience, social psychology, and medical anthropology. target_learning_goals: Understand and counteract stigmatizing beliefs about people with mental illness
examples: The pilot trial structured PWLE recovery narratives and aspirational figure discussions around the three stigma domains of survival, social, and professional threats
